title: WHY DID GOD COMMAND 12 STONES TO BE TAKEN FROM THE JORDAN RIVER? THE ANSWER IS MORE PERSONAL THAN YOU THINK.
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD COMMAND 12 STONES TO BE TAKEN FROM THE JORDAN RIVER? THE ANSWER IS MORE PERSONAL THAN YOU THINK.

They were just twelve ordinary stones pulled from a riverbed. But behind them was a miracle, a generation's painful history, and a message God refused to let His people forget. And once you understand why He commanded those stones to be carried, you may never look at your own journey through suffering the same way again.
There is something deeply unsettling about the way human beings remember.
We can remember one person who betrayed us twenty years ago, yet somehow forget a hundred times God showed us mercy.
We can replay the words that shattered our confidence, the relationship that fell apart, the prayers that seemed unanswered, and the night we almost gave up.
But the moment God brings us through something we once thought would destroy us?
We celebrate.
We cry.
We thank Him.
And then, slowly, we forget.
Not necessarily because we stopped believing.
Sometimes because life keeps moving, new battles arrive, and yesterday's miracle becomes today's distant memory.
And perhaps that is why one of the most extraordinary moments in the Old Testament did not end with a celebration.
It ended with twelve men carrying rocks.
Not gold.
Not weapons.
Not trophies taken from an enemy.
Just twelve stones from the bottom of a river.
And God Himself commanded it.
Why?
Because the miracle was never supposed to disappear when the water returned.
And neither was the testimony.
In Joshua chapter 4, Israel stood at a moment that would change its history forever.
Forty years of wilderness wandering were coming to an end.

A generation had died in the desert. Moses, the servant of the LORD who had led Israel out of Egypt, was gone. Joshua now carried the responsibility of leading the people into the land God had promised their ancestors.
But between the people and the land stood the Jordan River.
And Scripture gives us a detail that makes the scene even more remarkable.
Joshua 3:15 explains that the Jordan overflowed its banks during the harvest season.
This was not a convenient little stream the Israelites could casually step across.
The river was swollen.
The crossing was dangerous.
And an entire nation stood before it.
Imagine the mothers holding their children.
The elderly remembering the wilderness.
The younger generation staring at a river they could not simply command to move.
They had heard about the Red Sea.
They had heard how God delivered their fathers and mothers from Egypt.
But now they were standing before their own impossible crossing.
And that is where the story begins to reach beyond ancient history and into the places of our own lives we rarely talk about.
Because hearing someone else's testimony is not the same as standing in front of your own Jordan.
It is one thing to believe God delivered someone else.
It is another thing to trust Him when the obstacle is directly in front of you.
When the medical report is yours.
When the marriage is yours.
When the financial pressure is yours.
When the grief is yours.
When the future looks nothing like what you prayed for.
And when the next step of obedience seems frighteningly close to the very thing you fear.
Yet God did not tell Israel to build a bridge.
He told the priests carrying the ark of the covenant to move forward.
Joshua 3:13 records the promise that when the soles of the priests' feet rested in the Jordan, its waters would be cut off.
The ark represented the covenant presence of the LORD among His people. It was not a magical object, and the priests were not performing a human trick to control nature.
The living God was leading His people.
Then something extraordinary happened.
As the priests entered the river, the waters flowing from upstream stopped and stood in a heap far away, near Adam, the city beside Zarethan. The waters flowing toward the Dead Sea were cut off.
And Israel crossed on dry ground.
Not because the people were powerful enough to defeat the river.
Not because Joshua possessed some extraordinary ability independent of God.
But because the LORD had made a way.
The priests stood firm in the middle of the Jordan while the nation passed over.
Think about that.
The place that should have swallowed them became the ground beneath their feet.
The obstacle they could not overcome became the setting in which God's faithfulness was displayed.
And then, before the priests were permitted to leave the riverbed, God gave another command.
One that might have seemed strange in the middle of such an extraordinary moment.
Take twelve stones.
One for each tribe of Israel.
Carry them out of the Jordan.
And set them up where the people would spend the night.
Why would God interrupt such a monumental crossing to make men carry stones?
Because God was not only bringing Israel into a new place.
He was teaching Israel how to remember the One who brought them there.

Joshua 4:6–7 explains the purpose. The stones would become a sign among the people. When their children asked what the stones meant, their parents were to tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD.
The stones were to be a memorial to the people of Israel forever.
That word memorial matters.
In Joshua 4:7, the Hebrew expression is לְזִכָּרוֹן — lezikaron, meaning "for a memorial" or "as a remembrance."
It comes from the Hebrew root זכר — zakhar, associated with remembering.
The stones were not sacred objects possessing miraculous power.
They were not charms against future suffering.
They were not monuments to Israel's greatness.
They were physical witnesses to what the LORD had done.
And here is something that deserves your attention.
God knew that a generation could experience a miracle and still fail to pass its meaning to the next generation.
Children would be born who had never seen the Jordan stop flowing.
They would walk through a land they had not conquered themselves.
They would enjoy blessings whose beginnings they had not personally witnessed.
And eventually, one of them would look at those stones and ask:
"What do these mean?"
That question was not an interruption.
It was the purpose.
God was giving parents an opportunity to speak.
To remember.
To explain.
To testify.
Not simply, "We crossed a river."
But, "The LORD made a way for us."
And that difference changes everything.
Because a testimony that glorifies the person who survived can easily become a story about human strength.
But a testimony that glorifies God becomes a witness to divine faithfulness.
The twelve stones were not saying, "Look what we accomplished."
They were saying, "Remember what the LORD has done."
There is another detail in this account that is often overlooked.
Joshua 4:8 records that the twelve appointed men carried twelve stones out of the Jordan, according to the number of the tribes of Israel, and brought them to the place where the people lodged.
Later, Joshua 4:20 identifies Gilgal as the place where Joshua set up those twelve stones.
But Joshua 4:9 also tells us something surprising.
Joshua set up another twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, at the place where the feet of the priests carrying the ark had stood.
The Hebrew text distinguishes these actions, and the passage is most naturally read as describing stones taken out of the river and stones set up within it.
The account does not explain every detail of the second arrangement, so we should not invent hidden meanings God has not revealed.
But we should notice what Scripture actually says.
There were stones carried into Israel's new chapter.
And there were stones placed where the priests had stood during the crossing.
The narrative draws our attention both to the miracle and to the place where God had sustained His people.
One memorial stood in the land.
Another was placed in the riverbed.
And while the text does not tell us to turn every stone into an allegory, the historical picture is unforgettable.
Israel's future was not meant to be separated from the memory of God's faithfulness.
The people were moving forward.
But they were not supposed to move forward as though they had brought themselves there.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because some of us have become so consumed with reaching the next blessing that we have forgotten the God who carried us through the last battle.
We begged Him for another chance.
And He gave us another chance.
We cried when nobody else could hear us.
And He sustained us.
We asked Him to help us endure one more day.
And somehow, by His mercy, we reached the morning.
Yet now, when a new difficulty appears, we speak as though God has never been faithful before.
Our fear becomes louder than our memory.
Our circumstances become bigger than our theology.
And the enemy does not even need to convince us that God does not exist.
Sometimes all that needs to happen is for us to forget what He has already done.
But Scripture calls us back to remembrance.
Psalm 77:11 declares:
"I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old." (KJV)
Notice the determination.
"I will remember."
Not merely, "I remember when life feels easy."
Not, "I remember when every prayer is answered the way I wanted."
But, "I will remember."
Biblical remembrance is not pretending that pain never happened.
It is refusing to allow pain to erase the truth of who God is.
And maybe you need that reminder today.
Because some of you are reading this with a heart full of things nobody knows about.
You smile in photographs, but your mind is exhausted.
You encourage everyone else, but your own faith feels bruised.
You have learned how to say, "I'm okay," with such convincing calm that people have stopped asking.
And perhaps the most painful part is that you remember a season when trusting God felt easier.
Before the disappointment.
Before the betrayal.
Before the funeral.
Before the unanswered prayer.
Before the mistake you still struggle to forgive yourself for.
Now you are standing before another Jordan, wondering whether you have enough faith left to keep walking.
Listen carefully.
The power that divided the Jordan did not originate in the strength of the people crossing it.
It came from the LORD.
And the hope of the Gospel does not rest on your ability to manufacture perfect faith.
It rests on Jesus Christ, the faithful Savior who calls sinners to repent, trust Him, and receive His grace.
That does not mean every river in your life will part.
Not every illness is healed in this lifetime.
Not every broken relationship is restored.
Not every financial crisis disappears overnight.
And we must never turn Joshua 4 into a promise that every believer will receive the exact earthly outcome they desire.
God's promises to Israel at the Jordan were part of a particular covenant moment in redemptive history.
But the character of the God who kept His word has not changed.
And for those who belong to Christ, His ultimate promise is not a life without suffering.
It is redemption, resurrection, and everlasting life through His Son.
That is a far greater hope than a trouble-free journey.
There is something else we must understand about the twelve stones.
They represented twelve tribes.
Not twelve perfect tribes.
Not twelve groups of people who had never doubted, complained, rebelled, or sinned.
Israel's wilderness history contained painful examples of unbelief and disobedience.
And yet the twelve stones testified to the LORD's covenant faithfulness.
The memorial was not a celebration of Israel's moral perfection.
It was a witness to the mercy and faithfulness of God.
Does that sound familiar?
Because the Gospel begins with the uncomfortable truth that none of us can stand before God boasting of our righteousness.
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." (KJV)
All.
The respectable.
The religious.
The ashamed.
The wounded.
The person who has hidden a secret for years.
The person who thinks they have already ruined too much to be forgiven.
Every one of us needs grace.
And that is where this ancient river crossing begins to illuminate something far greater.
The twelve stones were a memorial of God's deliverance.
But the Bible's story does not end at Gilgal.
It moves forward through Israel's history, through the prophets, and ultimately to Jesus Christ.
And here we must be careful to honor the actual meaning of Scripture.
Joshua 4 does not explicitly say that the twelve stones symbolize the twelve apostles, the wounds of Jesus, or twelve specific stages of Christian salvation.
Those interpretations may sound dramatic, but we should not present imaginative connections as though God Himself declared them.
The original purpose of the stones was clear: Israel was to remember and proclaim the LORD's miraculous deliverance at the Jordan.
Yet within the larger story of Scripture, that deliverance belongs to the history that leads us toward Christ.
The God who brought His covenant people through the Jordan would ultimately fulfill His saving purposes through the promised Messiah.
And Jesus accomplished a deliverance far deeper than crossing a river.
He came to rescue sinners from sin and death.
At the cross, the innocent Son of God suffered for the guilty.
The One who knew no sin bore our sins.
The One who deserved worship endured rejection.
And the One whose death looked like defeat rose again in victory.
The Greek New Testament gives us a powerful word for grace.
χάρις — charis.
Grace.
God's undeserved favor.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (KJV)
This is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of people becoming strong enough to save themselves.
It is the story of the Savior who came for people who could not save themselves.
And this is where the message of the stones becomes deeply personal.
Because perhaps your past contains something you wish you could erase.
A decision that cost you years.
A relationship you damaged.
A season of rebellion.
An addiction you kept secret.
A betrayal.
A failure.
A version of yourself you can barely bear to remember.
And perhaps you have spent years believing that your story will always be defined by that chapter.
But the Gospel announces that your sin does not have to be the final word.
Jesus Christ calls us not to hide our sins, excuse them, or pretend they were harmless.
He calls us to repentance and faith.
And He offers forgiveness through His finished work.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Not because our confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because our tears earn salvation.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient.
And when grace meets repentance, something extraordinary happens.
The past is not magically rewritten as though evil were good.
The damage of sin is not dismissed.
Consequences may remain.
Relationships may require long seasons of rebuilding.
But in Christ, condemnation does not have to be the end of the story.
That is what we mean when we say:
He does not call darkness light.
He brings sinners out of darkness into His marvelous light.
He does not tell us that rebellion was harmless.
He forgives repentant rebels and begins transforming their lives.
He does not erase every painful memory.
He gives us a new identity and a future grounded in His mercy.
And that is a miracle worth remembering.
There is a reason the stones were intended to provoke questions from children.
Faithful testimony is not meant to die with the generation that experienced God's help.
Somewhere, a child needs to hear how God sustained a mother who almost gave up.
Somewhere, a son needs to know that his father was not always the man he is today, and that the mercy of Christ transformed his life.
Somewhere, a daughter needs to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and nobody is beyond the reach of the Gospel while they still have breath to turn to Christ.
Somewhere, a person who has never entered a church may encounter the first honest testimony of God's grace through a story shared on a phone.
And that is why telling the truth about what God has done matters.
Not every testimony needs to be dramatic.
You do not need to have survived a public scandal to glorify Christ.
Sometimes the testimony is that you were proud, and God humbled you.
You were bitter, and He taught you to forgive.
You were spiritually indifferent, and the Gospel awakened you.
You were tempted to abandon your faith, and God sustained you through His Word and the encouragement of His people.
Sometimes the testimony is simply this:
"I am still following Jesus, not because life has been easy, but because His grace has been sufficient."
And that may be exactly what another struggling believer needs to hear.
So I want to ask you something personal.
If someone asked you today, "What has God done in your life that you never want to forget?" what would you say?
Would you remember His provision?
His correction?
His patience?
His forgiveness?
The person He used to encourage you?
The Scripture that kept you grounded when everything else felt unstable?
The day you finally stopped running from the truth?
Do not despise those memories.
And do not confuse remembering God's faithfulness with glorifying the suffering itself.
The wounds were real.
The losses were real.
The sin was real.
But so was the mercy that met you there.
You may never build a monument of twelve stones.
You may never stand on the banks of the Jordan.
But you can speak truthfully about the Lord's faithfulness.
You can teach your children the Scriptures.
You can encourage someone with the Gospel.
You can tell the story of what Christ has done without making yourself the hero.
And when you do, your testimony can point beyond your circumstances to the Savior.
You do not have to expose private details or wounds you are not ready to discuss.
Maybe your words are simply:
"Christ is still healing me."
Maybe they are:
"I'm still fighting the good fight of faith."
Or perhaps:
"Jesus, teach me to remember Your faithfulness."
Because sometimes a person who feels completely alone needs to discover that other believers are willing to pray alongside them.
And sometimes the testimony you almost kept silent becomes the encouragement another person desperately needed.
Think about the people in your life who are facing their own Jordan.
The friend who has stopped going to church.
The family member who has grown cold toward God.
The person who carries shame and assumes Jesus would never welcome them.
The believer who is exhausted from fighting temptation.
The seeker who has questions but does not know whom to ask.
Not because a social media share earns God's favor.
Not because sharing a post makes anyone more righteous.
But because the truth of Jesus Christ deserves to be proclaimed, and even an ordinary act of sharing can become an opportunity for someone to hear the Gospel.
Because the message is too important to keep to ourselves.
And for those who believe in this mission and want to help it grow, there is another invitation.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing words that stir emotions for a moment.
Our desire is to point people toward the Word of God, help believers mature in Christ, encourage those who are spiritually weary, and reach people who may never otherwise stop to consider the Gospel.
We want these resources and messages to continue reaching families, struggling believers, seekers, and people who are hungry for biblical truth.
And that kind of ongoing work benefits from faithful support.
It should not be confused with purchasing God's blessing, earning spiritual favor, or replacing the responsibility to support your local church and other obligations you prayerfully recognize.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we extend this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But an opportunity for those who value this mission to help it continue.
You can pray for this ministry.
You can read and share the free resources.
You can participate in conversations that encourage repentance, faith, spiritual growth, and hope in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel itself is not for sale.
Christ's grace cannot be purchased.
Our deepest desire is not merely to gain another supporter.
It is to see another person know Jesus, trust His Word, turn from sin, and grow in the transforming grace of God.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the river.
Imagine Joshua standing on the other side.
The people have crossed.
The priests have completed their assignment.
The stones have been carried.
The miracle is finished.
And according to Joshua 4:18, when the priests bearing the ark came up from the Jordan, the waters returned to their place and overflowed the banks as before.
The river began flowing again.
The visible pathway disappeared.
Anyone arriving later might see nothing but an ordinary river.
They would not see the dry ground.
They would not hear the footsteps of an entire nation crossing.
They would not witness the priests standing in the riverbed.
But there would be stones at Gilgal.
And when someone asked what those stones meant, Israel had an answer.
The LORD had brought them through.
That is the beauty of the memorial.
The evidence of the miracle was not dependent on the river remaining divided forever.
God had made a way, and the people were commanded to remember.
Joshua 4:24 gives the ultimate purpose of this testimony:
"That all the people of the earth might know the hand of the LORD, that it is mighty: that ye might fear the LORD your God for ever." (KJV)
Do you see it?
The stones were never merely about Israel remembering its past.
They were about the nations knowing the mighty hand of the LORD.
They were about reverence.
They were about testimony.
They were about the glory of God.
And that purpose challenges us today.
When you tell your story, whom do people see?
Only the strength of the survivor?
Only the pain of the victim?
Only the success of the person who overcame?
Or do they see the mercy of the Savior?
Because the most beautiful testimony is not necessarily the one with the most shocking past.
It is the one that most faithfully magnifies Jesus Christ.
Maybe the waters in your life have not parted.
Maybe you are still waiting.
Maybe your prayers are still mixed with tears.
Do not manufacture a happy ending just to make your testimony sound impressive.
Keep trusting Christ.
Keep listening to His Word.
Keep walking in repentance and obedience.
Keep receiving the support of His people.
And remember that even when earthly circumstances remain unresolved, the resurrection of Jesus Christ gives believers a hope that suffering cannot ultimately destroy.
The empty tomb is not a symbol of wishful thinking.
It is the foundation of the Christian proclamation that Jesus Christ has conquered death.
And because He lives, those who belong to Him have a future that reaches beyond every grave, every sorrow, and every earthly disappointment.
The Jordan stones testified that God had brought Israel through a river.
The Gospel proclaims that through Jesus Christ, God brings repentant sinners from death to life.
And if Christ has redeemed you, your greatest testimony is not merely that you survived what happened to you.
It is that the Savior has shown you mercy.
So before another day passes, remember.
Remember His holiness.
Remember your need for grace.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the forgiveness offered through Jesus Christ.
And when the next generation asks what your faith means, do not give them only religious phrases.
Tell them the truth.
Tell them who Jesus is.
Tell them what He has done.
Tell them why you trust Him.
Tell them that grace is not permission to remain in sin, but the gift of God that leads us into a new life of faith and obedience.
Tell them that no scandal is too complicated for the Gospel to confront, and no repentant sinner is beyond the saving power of Christ.
And if this message has reached a place in your heart you have been afraid to open, do not simply close the page and return to pretending.
Speak to the Lord.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
"Jesus, don't let me forget what You've done."
Someone may read those words and realize they are not the only person learning to trust God again.
Not to purchase grace.
But because grace, freely received, can move grateful hearts to serve and give.
The stones were ordinary.
The God who delivered His people was not.
And the greatest hope of all is that the same faithful God has revealed His saving grace through Jesus Christ.
The river may cover the place where God carried you through, but it can never erase the faithfulness of the One who brought you there.
